title: Find the GCD (Greatest Common Divisor) of two numbers using Euclidean algorithm (`gcd(a,b) = gcd(b, a%b)`, base: `gcd(a,0) = a`).
shortTitle: Find the GCD of Two Numbers Using the Euclidean Algorithm

s1_definition.profdef: The greatest common divisor of two integers is the largest positive integer that divides both of them without a remainder. The Euclidean algorithm computes it efficiently by repeatedly replacing the pair with the smaller number and the remainder of dividing the larger by the smaller, using the identity that the GCD of a and b equals the GCD of b and a modulo b, until the remainder becomes zero, at which point the other number is the answer. It runs in logarithmic time in the size of the inputs.
s1_definition.analogy: Suppose the National Bank of India wants to pay out a dividend of a certain total to Rajesh and a certain total to Priya, and it only has notes of one denomination that must divide both totals exactly with none left over. The largest such note value is the greatest common divisor. Euclid's trick is like laying the smaller amount against the larger repeatedly, each time keeping only the leftover, until nothing is left over, and the last non-zero amount is the biggest note that fits both perfectly.
s1_definition.oneliner: Keep replacing the pair with the smaller number and the remainder until the remainder is zero; the last non-zero number is the GCD.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The greatest common divisor of two integers is the largest positive integer that divides both of them without a remainder. The Euclidean algorithm computes it efficiently by repeatedly replacing the pair with the smaller number and the remainder of dividing the larger by the smaller, using the identity that the GCD of a and b equals the GCD of b and a modulo b, until the remainder becomes zero, at which point the other number is the answer. It runs in logarithmic time in the size of the inputs.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Suppose the National Bank of India wants to pay out a dividend of a certain total to Rajesh and a certain total to Priya, and it only has notes of one denomination that must divide both totals exactly with none left over. The largest such note value is the greatest common divisor. Euclid's trick is like laying the smaller amount against the larger repeatedly, each time keeping only the leftover, until nothing is left over, and the last non-zero amount is the biggest note that fits both perfectly.

**One line to remember:** Keep replacing the pair with the smaller number and the remainder until the remainder is zero; the last non-zero number is the GCD.

sections.s2_technical:
The identity at the heart of this is that the greatest common divisor of two numbers does not change if you replace the larger by its remainder when divided by the smaller. Formally, the GCD of a and b equals the GCD of b and a modulo b. The base case is that the GCD of a and zero is a, because every number divides zero and the largest divisor of a is a itself.

You can write this recursively or iteratively. The recursive version reads almost exactly like the mathematical identity: if b is zero return a, otherwise return the GCD of b and a modulo b. For example `gcd(48, 36)` calls `gcd(36, 12)` calls `gcd(12, 0)` which returns `12`. The iterative version uses a while loop: while b is not zero, hold the old b in a temporary, set b to a modulo b, and set a to the temporary, then return a at the end.

A senior point is performance. The number of steps is bounded logarithmically; in the worst case, which happens for consecutive Fibonacci numbers, it is still very fast. This is far better than trying every candidate divisor downward, which would be linear in the smaller number.

Another senior point is handling negatives and zero. The GCD is usually defined as non-negative, so I take the absolute value of each input first. The GCD of zero and zero is conventionally zero or undefined; I return zero and document it. In banking the inputs are positive amounts or counts, but defending the edges is good practice.

A related idea is the least common multiple, which you get cheaply once you have the GCD: the LCM of a and b equals a divided by the GCD, multiplied by b. Dividing first avoids overflow. For example the LCM of 4 and 6 is 4 divided by 2, which is 2, times 6, which is 12.

A small finance-domain example: `int a = 48, b = 36; while (b != 0) { int t = b; b = a % b; a = t; } int gcd = a;` which leaves `gcd` as `12`, the largest coin value dividing both payout totals.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a loyalty cashback scheme where Rajesh has accumulated one amount of reward points converted to rupees and Priya another amount. The bank wants to disburse both as physical vouchers of a single denomination, and it wants the largest denomination that divides both totals exactly so that no fractional voucher is ever needed. Finding that largest denomination is exactly the greatest common divisor of the two totals.

This is exactly how the Euclidean algorithm works in Java — we feed the two totals in and repeatedly reduce using remainder until one becomes zero, and the survivor is the biggest denomination that fits both.

Problem 2 — The bank also schedules two recurring fee charges, one that recurs every so many days and another every so many days, and the operations team wants to know after how many days both fees fall on the same day again, which is the least common multiple of the two periods. Once we have the GCD, the LCM is a cheap one-line follow-up, dividing by the GCD first to avoid overflow.

What the code will do: a `DenominationService` class with a `gcd(long a, long b)` method (iterative Euclid), a `lcm(long a, long b)` method built on top of it, and a demo that computes the largest voucher denomination for Rajesh's and Priya's cashback and the day both fees realign.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's cashback is `4800` and Priya's cashback is `3600`.

Step 1: Both values enter `gcd`. We take absolute values, which leaves them unchanged. We enter the loop with a equal to `4800` and b equal to `3600`.

Step 2: First turn. `temp` holds `3600`. The remainder `4800 % 3600` is `1200`, so b becomes `1200`. Then a becomes `temp`, which is `3600`.

Step 3: Second turn. `temp` holds `1200`. The remainder `3600 % 1200` is `0`, so b becomes `0`. Then a becomes `temp`, which is `1200`.

Step 4: The loop condition b not equal to zero is now false, so the loop stops. a holds `1200`, which is returned as the GCD. That is the largest voucher denomination that divides both cashback totals exactly.

Step 5: For the fee realignment, `lcm(12, 18)` first computes `gcd(12, 18)`. The loop reduces `(12,18)` to `(18,12)` to `(12,6)` to `(6,0)`, giving GCD `6`. Then the LCM is `12 / 6 * 18 = 2 * 18 = 36`.

Step 6: The final answers are a voucher denomination of `1200` rupees and a fee realignment after `36` days. Neither input amount was mutated outside the method; the method consumed local copies.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T14:20:00Z INFO Largest voucher denomination for Rs.4800 and Rs.3600 = Rs.1200
2026-10-26T14:20:00Z INFO Fees of every 12 and 18 days realign after 36 days
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: Rajesh cashback 4800, Priya cashback 3600
    │
    ▼
  gcd(4800, 3600)
    │ turn1: temp=3600 b=4800%3600=1200 a=3600
    │ turn2: temp=1200 b=3600%1200=0    a=1200
    │ b==0 → stop
    ▼
  GCD = 1200  (largest voucher denomination)
    │
    ├─ fee path: lcm(12,18)
    │   gcd(12,18)=6 → 12/6*18 = 36 days
    ▼
  Output: denomination Rs.1200; fees realign after 36 days
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The greatest common divisor of two integers is the largest positive integer that divides both with no remainder, and the Euclidean algorithm is the efficient way to find it. The key identity is that the GCD of a and b equals the GCD of b and the remainder of a divided by b, with the base case that the GCD of any number and zero is that number. I usually code it iteratively with a while loop that keeps replacing the pair until the second value becomes zero, and then the first value is the answer.

The reason I prefer Euclid over trying every candidate divisor downward is performance. Euclid runs in logarithmic time in the size of the inputs, with the worst case being consecutive Fibonacci numbers, whereas the brute-force divisor search is linear in the smaller number. I also take absolute values up front so the result is well defined for any sign, and I document that the GCD of zero and zero is returned as zero.

Once I have the GCD I get the least common multiple almost for free, because the LCM of a and b is a divided by the GCD, times b. I always divide before multiplying so that the intermediate value does not overflow, which matters when the numbers are large, as banking amounts can be.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used the GCD to pick the largest single voucher denomination that divides both Rajesh's and Priya's cashback totals exactly, so operations never needs a fractional voucher, and I used the LCM to work out after how many days two recurring fee charges fall on the same day again. Explaining it with those two concrete uses shows the interviewer that I understand both the math identity and why it matters in a real scheduling and disbursement context.
